questions.question: What is abstraction in Java and how is it achieved?
questions.title: Abstraction in Java Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Abstraction** is the OOP principle of hiding implementation details and exposing only the essential interface. In Java, abstraction is achieved through **abstract classes** (partial abstraction) and **interfaces** (full abstraction, or partial since Java 8). It lets callers work with a concept without knowing how it's implemented.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of WHY abstraction exists — not just the syntax, but the principle of separating interface from implementation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing abstraction with encapsulation — abstraction hides complexity/implementation, encapsulation hides data
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world analogy: you drive a car using the steering wheel without knowing how the engine works — that's abstraction

sections.title: Hiding Complexity, Showing Essentials
sections.content:
Abstraction is about showing what an object does, not how it does it. Think of a TV remote: you press buttons and the TV responds. You don't know the infrared signal frequency, the circuit that processes it, or the firmware — that's all abstracted away.

In Java, two mechanisms achieve abstraction:

**1. Abstract classes** — partial abstraction (can have abstract + concrete methods):
```java
abstract class Vehicle {
    abstract void start();      // WHAT — subclass decides HOW
    void fuel() { System.out.println("Using fuel"); }  // concrete: HOW provided
}
```

**2. Interfaces** — full contract (purely WHAT, no state):
```java
interface Printable {
    void print(String content); // just the contract
}
```

The caller writes code against `Vehicle` or `Printable` without caring whether the underlying impl is a `Car`, `ElectricBike`, `PDFPrinter`, or `NetworkPrinter`. Implementation details are hidden.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Abstraction: show WHAT, hide HOW
- Achieved via `abstract` classes and `interface`
- Abstract class: can have abstract methods (no body) + concrete methods
- Interface: defines a contract — all methods are abstract by default (pre-Java 8)
- Java 8+ interfaces can have `default` and `static` methods with bodies
- Abstraction enables swappable implementations (polymorphism + dependency injection)
- Reduces coupling: caller depends on abstraction, not concrete type

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Abstraction in Java means hiding the complexity of how something works and exposing only what it does. The analogy I like is a TV remote — you press 'volume up' and it works; you don't need to know the IR signal or the firmware. In Java, we achieve abstraction through abstract classes and interfaces. Abstract classes provide partial abstraction — they can have abstract methods that subclasses must implement, plus concrete methods. Interfaces provide full abstraction — they define contracts. The benefit is that your code works against the abstraction, so you can swap implementations without changing any calling code.

questions.question: What is an abstract class in Java and what are its characteristics?
questions.title: Abstract Class in Java — Characteristics and Usage
questions.direct_answer: An **abstract class** is declared with the `abstract` keyword and **cannot be instantiated**. It can have abstract methods (no body — subclasses must implement), concrete methods (with body), fields, and constructors. It is used when you want to provide partial implementation and force subclasses to complete the rest.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of when and why to use abstract classes — not just the syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying abstract classes cannot have constructors or fields — they can have both
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Template Method pattern: abstract class defines the algorithm skeleton with some steps abstract — subclasses fill in the details

sections.title: Abstract Class — Partial Implementation Blueprint
Key Points
sections.content:
- `abstract` keyword on class declaration
- **Cannot be instantiated** — `new AbstractClass()` is a compile error
- Can have `abstract` methods (no body) — subclasses must implement
- Can have **concrete methods** (with body), **fields**, and **constructors**
- A class with even one abstract method must be declared abstract
- If a subclass doesn't implement all abstract methods, it must also be abstract
- Abstract class reference can hold a subclass object: `Shape s = new Circle()`
- Use case: Template Method pattern, sharing common code with enforced overrides

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: An abstract class is declared with the `abstract` keyword and cannot be instantiated directly. It can contain abstract methods that have no body — subclasses are forced to provide the implementation — as well as concrete methods, fields, and constructors. A common use is the Template Method pattern: the abstract class defines the overall algorithm in a concrete method and delegates specific steps to abstract methods that subclasses implement. If a subclass doesn't implement all abstract methods, it must itself be declared abstract.

questions.question: What are the rules for abstract methods in Java?
questions.title: Rules for Abstract Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: Abstract methods have **no body**, are declared with the `abstract` keyword, must be in an `abstract class` or `interface`, and **must be overridden** by the first concrete (non-abstract) subclass. They cannot be `private`, `static`, or `final` — all of which would prevent overriding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the constraints on abstract methods and why private/static/final are incompatible
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking abstract methods can be private (they can't — private methods can't be overridden)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the reasoning: abstract methods exist to be overridden; any modifier that prevents overriding is incompatible with abstract

sections.title: Abstract Method Rules and Constraints
Key Points
sections.content:
- Abstract method: no body, ends with semicolon
- Cannot be `private` (blocks overriding), `static` (class-level, not polymorphic), or `final` (prevents overriding)
- Can be `public` or `protected`
- Must be in an `abstract class` or `interface`
- First concrete subclass MUST implement all abstract methods
- If a subclass provides partial implementation, it must also be `abstract`
- Interfaces: all methods are implicitly abstract (pre-Java 8) unless `default` or `static`
- Abstract method signature must match exactly in the implementing subclass

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Abstract methods have no body — just the signature ending with a semicolon — and they must be in an abstract class or interface. The first concrete subclass must override all abstract methods. The modifiers that are incompatible with abstract are private, static, and final — and the reason is the same for all three: abstract methods exist to be overridden, and these modifiers prevent overriding. Private hides the method from subclasses, static binds it to the class, and final locks it. Abstract methods can be public or protected.

questions.question: What were the changes to interfaces in Java 8 and why were they added?
questions.title: Java 8 Interface Changes — Default and Static Methods
questions.direct_answer: Java 8 added **default methods** (concrete methods in interfaces with the `default` keyword) and **static methods** to interfaces. This allowed adding new methods to existing interfaces **without breaking all implementing classes** — a major API evolution problem that had no clean solution before Java 8.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Java 8 features and understanding the motivation behind default methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing WHY default methods were added — just knowing the syntax without the context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the diamond problem with default methods and that Java resolves it by requiring the implementing class to override the conflicting method

sections.title: Default Methods — Interface Evolution Without Breaking Changes
Key Points
sections.content:
- `default` methods: concrete methods in interfaces, implementing classes inherit them
- `static` methods in interfaces: utility methods, called via `InterfaceName.method()`
- Primary motivation: evolve existing interfaces (like `Collection`, `Iterable`) without breaking existing code
- Implementing class can override a default method if needed
- If two interfaces provide conflicting default methods, implementing class MUST override
- Java 9 added `private` methods in interfaces (for reuse within the interface)
- Abstract class still preferred over interface when you need state (fields) or constructors

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java 8 added default methods and static methods to interfaces. The main reason was to allow the JDK itself to evolve — specifically to add methods like `stream()` and `forEach()` to the `Collection` and `Iterable` interfaces without breaking the millions of classes that already implemented those interfaces. Default methods have a body and are inherited by implementing classes automatically. One complication: if two interfaces provide conflicting default methods, the implementing class must explicitly override and resolve the conflict — Java won't do it automatically.

questions.question: Can you instantiate an abstract class in Java?
questions.title: Can You Instantiate an Abstract Class in Java?
questions.direct_answer: No, you **cannot directly instantiate** an abstract class — `new AbstractClass()` is a compile error. However, you can create an **anonymous class** that instantiates and provides implementations for all abstract methods inline. In normal usage, you instantiate a concrete subclass and use the abstract class as the reference type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the no-instantiation rule and awareness of anonymous classes as an exception
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about anonymous classes, or thinking abstract classes can never be used at all in object creation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the anonymous class syntax and mention it's commonly used with comparators and event handlers

sections.title: No Direct Instantiation — But Anonymous Classes Work
Key Points
sections.content:
- `new AbstractClass()` → compile error: 'Cannot instantiate abstract class'
- Can use abstract class as a **reference type**: `Shape s = new Circle()`
- **Anonymous class**: `new AbstractClass() { /* implement abstract methods */ }` creates an unnamed subclass
- Anonymous classes were common pre-Java 8; lambda expressions largely replaced them for functional interfaces
- Abstract classes CAN have constructors — called by concrete subclass via `super()`
- The no-instantiation rule enforces that abstract behavior must be made concrete before use

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You cannot directly instantiate an abstract class — `new AbstractClass()` gives a compile error. But you can use it as a reference type to hold subclass objects, like `Shape s = new Circle()`. There's also the anonymous class technique: you can write `new AbstractClass() { implement abstract methods here }` which creates an unnamed concrete subclass on the spot. This was common for callbacks and listeners before Java 8, but lambda expressions have largely replaced it for single-method abstractions.

questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java and how does it relate to abstraction?
questions.title: Functional Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **functional interface** is an interface with exactly **one abstract method**. It can have `default` and `static` methods in addition. It is annotated with `@FunctionalInterface` (optional but recommended). Lambda expressions and method references can be used to provide the implementation of a functional interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of functional interfaces, lambda expressions, and the @FunctionalInterface annotation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @FunctionalInterface makes an interface functional — it just validates. The one-abstract-method rule is what makes it functional
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention built-in functional interfaces: Runnable, Callable, Comparator, Predicate<T>, Function<T,R>, Consumer<T>, Supplier<T>

sections.title: One Abstract Method = Functional Interface
Key Points
sections.content:
- Exactly one abstract method = functional interface
- `@FunctionalInterface` annotation: optional, but validates at compile time
- Can have multiple `default` and `static` methods
- Enables lambda expressions: `() -> ...`, `x -> ...`, `(x, y) -> ...`
- Key built-ins: `Predicate<T>`, `Function<T,R>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`, `Runnable`, `Comparator<T>`
- Lambdas are syntactic sugar for anonymous class implementing the single abstract method
- `Runnable` was a functional interface before Java 8 — now usable as lambda: `() -> doWork()`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation is optional but useful — it tells the compiler to verify the interface only has one abstract method. The significance of functional interfaces is that they can be implemented using lambda expressions, which are much more concise than anonymous classes. For example, `Runnable` is a functional interface — instead of creating an anonymous class, you can just write `() -> doSomething()`. The Java 8 standard library added many functional interfaces in the `java.util.function` package like `Predicate`, `Function`, `Consumer`, and `Supplier`.
